title: The Medium Is Not the Message
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: Mutually Assured Instruction pushes back against what the author sees as a growing cancellation campaign against PowerPoint and slide-deck instruction, arguing that attributing poor teaching to the medium is a fundamental category error. The article surveys five delivery methods -- slide decks, OneNote, document cameras/visualizers, chalk-and-talk, and inquiry learning -- analyzing what each looks like when used well vs. poorly, and finding consistently that the difference lies in teacher expertise rather than the medium itself. The author argues that research-backed effective teaching techniques (worked examples, live modelling, checking for understanding, building on prior knowledge) can be executed through almost any medium, while poor pedagogy makes any medium fail. Particular attention is given to inquiry learning, which the author acknowledges can produce rich learning with expert learners but becomes a 'recipe for inequity' when used with novices who lack the prerequisite knowledge to inquire meaningfully. The article's position is that medium debates are a distraction: the critical variable in every comparison is the teacher's expertise, not the tool through which it is expressed.
points: * The anti-PowerPoint critique confuses correlation with causation: mediocre teachers often use slide decks, but the slides do not cause the mediocrity -- swapping the medium while keeping the pedagogy unchanged will not improve student learning. * OneNote, when used well, creates a 'living and breathing page' that models expert annotation in real time, preserving the teacher's models permanently as a resource students can revisit; when used poorly, it is just words on a page with no meaningful generation of procedures. * Document cameras are uniquely effective for live think-alouds because they allow a teacher to seamlessly float between instruction, checking for understanding, and celebrating student exemplar responses without the pre-planning burden of slide decks. * Inquiry learning is not universally effective -- it requires learners with the prerequisite knowledge to ask meaningful questions and filter irrelevant information; with novices, unguided inquiry becomes 'a recipe for inequity' that widens the achievement gap as advantaged students navigate it and disadvantaged students cannot. * The critical variable across every medium comparison is teacher expertise: effective techniques (worked examples, live modelling, CFUs) can be deployed through slides, OneNote, chalk, or document camera -- the medium is a tool, the teacher is the argument.
quotes: This can create a living and breathing page which can ebb and flow with the needs of the students in front of the teacher on the day. If the students are unable to show understanding after a worked example, the teacher can easily create another directly next to it in the infinite space that OneNote provides. After the completion of instruction all of these models are then permanently etched into the class OneNote to be referred to in future.

A well used class with a document camera can seamlessly float between instruction, checking for understanding and celebrating student exemplar responses without as much pre-planning required for the teacher as a slide deck would. Even better is that most modern document cameras can record the video or key images of the completed models so that they can be kept for eternity.

A well delivered chalk and talk can sequentially build layers of understanding of a complex topic which never overloads working memory. Information only appears when it becomes relevant and all old information remains visible rather than transient. This can provide students with optimum opportunities to rehearse the content in hopes some may transfer to long term memory.

At the end of a lesson sequence with relative experts? That's amore. Inquiry with novices? That's a recipe for inequity. The reason why is that novices do not have the pre-requisite knowledge required to ask the questions needed to inquire meaningfully as well as filter the seductive details which may not be relevant to the required learning.

Well executed inquiry will ironically require one of the above explicit teaching methods executed to a high standard directly before it. This way the students have all of the required tools in their arsenal to ask the right questions and feel capable of diving deep into the learning while having the capacity to filter through sources of varying quality.

Sometimes a week of class time could be allocated to completing a research task and within that hour I'd argue that some students use half an hour or less of that time productively. That means that almost 10% of a terms potential learning is lost in the guise of having a student centred approach to learning.
